title: How to Have a Weekly Marriage Check-In
excerpt: Most marriages do not die in a blowup. They die in a hundred small things never said. A weekly check-in is how you keep the silence from accumulating.
body:
Most marriages do not end in a fight. They end in a drift no one decided on, a slow accumulation of things never said until two people are running a household and sleeping in the same bed and living in different countries. The weekly check-in is the cheapest insurance against that drift, and almost no one does it, because it feels formal, and because we tell ourselves we talk plenty. We do talk plenty. We just talk about logistics, and logistics is not the same as being known.

I did not invent this practice and I resisted it for years. It felt like scheduling intimacy, which sounds like a contradiction. Then I noticed that the things in my marriage that mattered most also got attention only when they exploded, and the things that ran on a schedule, the bills, the kids' appointments, did not explode. The schedule was not killing the romance. The absence of one was.

## What it is and what it is not

A check-in is not a date and it is not a counseling session. It is a short, regular, protected conversation, twenty to forty minutes, where the only agenda is the marriage itself. Not the kids' schedule. Not the broken dishwasher. The two of you, and how you are actually doing.

Pick a fixed time and defend it like a bill that is due. Sunday evening after the kids are down. Friday morning before work. The day matters less than the fact that it does not move. If it floats, it dies, because there will always be something more urgent, and a marriage that only gets the leftover scraps of exhausted attention will slowly starve on them.

## A simple structure

You need a structure because without one you will default to grievances or to logistics. Here is one that holds.

Start with gratitude. Each of you names one thing the other did this week that you noticed and were glad for. This is not a warm-up to soften the blow of the hard part. It is its own discipline. We become experts at cataloging our spouse's failures and amateurs at noticing their kindnesses, and the catalog we keep is the one that shapes how we see them. Name the kindness out loud and you train your own eye to look for it.

Then ask the real question. How are you, actually. Not the reflexive fine. How is your heart this week, where are you tired, where are you carrying something. Then the hard part, which is that you have to listen without fixing. Your spouse names a weight and every instinct in you wants to solve it. Resist. Most of the time they do not want the weight solved. They want it witnessed.

Then ask about the marriage directly. Is there anything between us right now. Anything I did this week that landed wrong, anything you have been sitting on. This is the question that prevents the slow buildup, the unaddressed bid, the small hurt that hardens into contempt if it is never spoken. Ask it every week and the grievances never get the chance to compound, because you keep the account short.

Then look forward. What does the coming week need from us, where will we be stretched thin, where do we need to cover for each other. This is the only place logistics belong, and even here, keep it brief.

## When it gets hard

The first few will be awkward. You will not know what to say. One of you will treat it like a performance review and the other will get defensive, and you will both wonder why you started. Stay with it. The awkwardness is not a sign it is failing. It is a sign you have not done this in a long time, maybe ever, and the muscle is weak.

If something surfaces that is too big for twenty minutes, do not try to resolve it in the check-in. Name it, agree to come back to it when you both have more in the tank, and move on. The check-in is not where you fight the war. It is where you notice the war is starting before it does damage.

Keep your spouse's dignity safe in this conversation no matter what comes up. The whole thing only works if it is safe, and it is only safe if honesty does not get used as a weapon later. If your spouse tells you something tender and you throw it back in an argument three days later, you have taught them never to be honest in the check-in again, and you have killed the one practice that could have saved you the trouble.

Scripture says do not let the sun go down on your anger. The check-in is that verse made into a weekly habit, a fast and reliable path back before the anger calcifies into something colder. Paul also tells us to be kind, tenderhearted, forgiving one another. A marriage is finally only as durable as its capacity to forgive, and forgiveness is easier when the account is short. The check-in keeps it short.

## This week

Pick the time before you finish reading this. Put it on both phones. Make the first one short, fifteen minutes, three questions: one thing I was grateful for this week, one thing I am carrying, one thing between us if there is anything. Do not aim for a perfect conversation. Aim for the first one. The marriages that last are not the ones that drifted less. They are the ones that learned to row back, and the check-in is the oar in your hand every single week.

title: How to Fight Fair
excerpt: The goal of a marital argument is not to win. A marriage where someone keeps winning is a marriage where someone keeps losing.
body:
The first lie about conflict in marriage is that good marriages do not have much of it. The couples who never fight are usually the ones where someone has gone underground, where the peace is being bought by one person swallowing themselves whole, and that bill always comes due with interest. Conflict is not the enemy of a marriage. Contempt is. Learning the difference may be the most practical skill a married person can develop.

You married a separate human being with a separate history and a separate set of wounds and a separate way of loading the dishwasher that is, you will discover, somehow morally wrong. You are going to fight. The question is never whether. The question is what the fight is for, and whether anyone walks out of it bleeding.

## Win the marriage, not the argument

The goal of a marital argument is not to win. I know the rush of landing the unanswerable point, the line your spouse cannot rebut, and I know how I feel an hour later, because I understand what I actually did. A marriage where someone keeps winning is a marriage where someone keeps losing, and you cannot build a covenant on a standing score. Every time you win the argument you lose a little of the marriage, until one day the losses add up to something you cannot pay.

The goal is to understand and be understood and to come out the other side still on the same team. Everything else is technique in service of that, or it is poison dressed up as technique.

## Fight the real thing

There is a difference between the thing you are fighting about and the thing you are fighting for. The thing you are fighting about is the credit card statement, the in-laws, the unmade plan. The thing you are fighting for is almost always one of a few deep things: to feel respected, to feel chosen, to feel that you are not carrying this alone, to feel safe. The surface fights are endless reruns of the same three or four underlying ones. Ask yourself, in the middle of it, what am I actually fighting for here, and you will sometimes find the statement was never the issue.

## The moves that turn a fight into a wound

Four behaviors corrode a marriage, and researchers who have watched thousands of couples confirm what Scripture always said about the corrosive tongue. I have watched all four nearly do damage in my own house.

Contempt is the worst. Anger says you hurt me. Contempt says you are beneath me. It comes out in the eye roll, the mocking tone, the of course you would. It does not attack a behavior, it attacks a person, and a person can only answer an attack on their worth by attacking back or going cold. Keep contempt out of your mouth. Your spouse's dignity stays off the table no matter how hot it gets.

The kitchen sink is the second, where the fight about tonight becomes the fight about everything and you reach back three years to haul up old grievances. Fight the thing in front of you. One issue. If the old things keep surfacing, that means they were buried, not resolved, but the middle of a new fight is not the place to exhume them.

The universal quantifier is the third. You always, you never. These are almost always false and your spouse knows it, so you hand them an easy out: they argue about the word always instead of the actual hurt. Drop it. Say what happened this time.

Stonewalling is the fourth and the sneakiest, because it does not look like aggression. Going silent. Walking out. Shutting the face into a wall. It feels like self-control to the one doing it and like abandonment to the one left behind. Sometimes you genuinely need to stop because you are flooded. Fine. But say it. I am too far gone to do this well right now, I am not leaving you, I need twenty minutes, and I will come back. The difference between a wise pause and a punishing silence is whether you promised to come back.

## Anger is not the sin

The church often shames anger and is frequently wrong to. Be angry and do not sin, Paul writes, which means the anger and the sin are separable. The issue is never that you feel it hot. The issue is what the heat does. Heat that burns the issue is fine. Heat that burns the person is not. If your volume makes your spouse go silent and small, then whatever it feels like from inside, from the outside it is working as a weapon, and love requires you to care more about the wound than the catharsis.

And to the one who avoids: peacekeeping is not peacemaking. The peacekeeper avoids the conflict to keep the surface calm. The peacemaker enters it to make a deeper peace on the other side. Jesus blessed the second one. If you keep the peace by never saying the hard thing, you are not protecting the marriage. You are starving it and calling the starvation kindness.

## The repair is what saves you

No couple fights perfectly. The healthy ones are not the ones who never cross the line. They are the ones who notice and come back. The repair can be small: a hand on the shoulder, a softer voice, I am sorry, that was beneath me, can we start over. Whether the repair gets received matters more than how bad the fight got. A marriage is not measured by the absence of rupture. It is measured by the speed of repair.

## This week

Next time you feel the fight starting, do one thing: before you respond, ask yourself what you are actually fighting for, and name that instead of the surface complaint. I am not angry about the dishes, I am feeling like I carry this house alone. Say the real thing. And if you cross a line, do not wait for a clean moment to repair. Repair badly and fast. The marriages that last are not the ones without wounds. They are the ones that learned to heal faster than they hurt.

title: How to Have the Money Conversation Without a War
excerpt: Money fights are almost never about money. They are about fear and control and worth, and a budget cannot fix a thing the budget cannot see.
body:
When couples come to me about money, they think they are coming about money. They have the numbers ready and they want me to adjudicate. I learned to set the numbers aside almost immediately, because in fifteen years of these conversations I have rarely met a money fight that was actually about money. The money is the surface. Underneath it, every time, is something older and more tender. Fear. Control. Worth. The childhood that taught you whether there would ever be enough.

You marry not just a person but a whole financial history you cannot see. One of you grew up watching the lights get shut off, and now a low balance does not register as a number, it registers as terror. The other grew up where money was always there and never discussed, and now the spouse's anxiety reads as irrational and controlling. Neither of you is being unreasonable given where you came from. You are each being faithful to a different god of money you were handed before you could choose, and now both gods live in the same account.

## Start with testimony, not the budget

The first work is not budgeting. It is testimony. Sit down, not in a fight, and tell each other the truth about money. What did money feel like in the house you grew up in. What were you afraid of. What did your parents do with it, and what did it teach you to expect. I have watched this one conversation do more for a marriage's finances than any spreadsheet, because once a man understands that his wife's frugality is a six-year-old standing in a cold house, he stops fighting the frugality and starts comforting the child.

Do not skip this and jump to the numbers. The numbers are downstream of the fear, and if you fight the numbers without understanding the fear, you will have the same fight again next month with different figures.

## Decide whether the money is ours

The single most important financial decision a married couple makes is whether the money is ours, not legally but in the heart, in the daily practice. There is a way of running finances that keeps a quiet wall down the middle, your money and my money, a careful ledger of who paid for what. I understand the instinct, especially for someone burned before. But that wall is a contract wall, and a covenant has no wall. The biblical picture is one flesh, and one flesh does not run two accounts and keep score.

I want to honor the real exception. If you are married to someone genuinely reckless or financially abusive, protecting yourself is wisdom, not faithlessness, and combining everything is not covenant but enabling. But for most couples the separate-accounts instinct is not guarding against a real danger. It is keeping a door cracked toward the exit, and the marriage feels that hedge even when no one names it.

## Build a plan with room to be an adult

Most daily friction lives in the question of who controls the spending. One person tracking the budget is fine. One person being the family's controller, approving the other's every purchase like a parent doling out lunch money, is not stewardship. It is a slow humiliation, and it lands hardest on the spouse who earns less or stays home. If your spouse cannot buy a coffee or a book without filing a request, you do not have a budget. You have a hierarchy, and you made yourself the throne.

The fix is a shared plan with room in it for each person to be a free adult. Decide the categories together, then within reason each of you gets to be trusted. Give each person a small no-questions-asked amount, equal regardless of who earns it. Trust is not a reward for good behavior. It is the air a marriage breathes.

## Name the hidden debt

Debt is the fault line that hides. A spouse opens a card, then another, covers the minimums, says nothing, and the shame of the first lie funds the second. By the time it surfaces the betrayal is not really about the dollars. It is about the months of looking you in the eye and hiding. Financial infidelity is a real category the church rarely names, and I have watched it break trust as deeply as the other kind.

If you are hiding money or debt from your spouse, the dollars are not your worst problem. The hiding is. The only way out is the one that costs you: bring it into the light before you are caught, say the whole number out loud, and let your spouse be angry without rushing them past it. There is no version where you keep the secret and keep the marriage whole.

## The deeper question money is always asking

A budget is a moral document whether you intend it or not. It is a record of what you worshiped, written in dollars, with no power to lie. So decide together not just how to spend but what the money is for. Security, status, the kids' every advantage, a house that announces something. Or held a little loosely, with generosity built in before the wants get their turn. Jesus said more about money than about heaven or hell, because he knew the heart attaches to money the way it should attach to God. You cannot serve both.

## This week

Schedule one hour, not to look at the budget, but to tell each other your money stories. Each of you answers two questions: what did money feel like growing up, and what are you most afraid of around money now. No fixing, no rebuttals, just listening. The budget can wait a week. Until you understand the fear under your spouse's number, every spreadsheet you build will be built on top of a wound the spreadsheet cannot see.

title: How to Repair After a Blowup
excerpt: Every marriage has bad fights. The ones that last are not the couples who never cross the line. They are the ones who come back fast.
body:
You said the thing. Maybe you yelled it, maybe you said it quietly in the voice that cuts deeper than yelling, and now the house has that specific silence in it, the one where two people are in the same building and a wall has gone up between them. Every marriage has these nights. The question is not whether you will have a bad fight. You will. The question is what you do in the hours after, because the repair is the part that actually saves a marriage, and almost no one is taught how to do it.

I have studied the people who come back from these well, and I have failed at it often enough in my own marriage to know the failure from the inside. Here is what I have learned.

## First, let the body come down

When a fight goes nuclear, both of you are flooded. The heart is up over a hundred beats a minute, the part of the brain that does empathy has gone offline, and the part that does survival is driving. You cannot repair from inside that state. Anything you say in the first minutes will be the survival brain talking, and it does not want peace, it wants to win or to flee.

So the first move is not words. It is time, and a promise. Not stonewalling, which is walking out in cold silence and leaving your spouse erased. The difference is one sentence: I am too flooded to do this well, I am not leaving you, I need some time, and I will come back. Then actually come back. Twenty minutes, an hour, but you set a time and you keep it. A pause without a promise is abandonment. A pause with a promise is mercy.

Use the time to come down, not to build your case. If you spend the break rehearsing your closing argument, you will come back more armed than before. Walk. Pray. Let the heart rate drop.

## Own your part first

When you come back, do not start with what they did. Start with what you did. This is the move that breaks the deadlock, and it is almost unbearable, because every cell in you wants the apology to flow the other direction first.

There is always a part that is yours. Even if you were ninety percent right about the issue, the way you said it, the contempt in your tone, the old grievance you dragged in, the silence you used to punish, some of that is yours, and you can confess it without conceding the whole argument. I am sorry I rolled my eyes at you. I am sorry I brought up your mother. I am sorry I went cold and made you chase me. Name the specific thing. A vague I am sorry if you were hurt is not a repair, it is a dodge.

Confession is not the same as caving on the issue. You can own how you fought and still hold what you believe about the substance. But you own your part first, and unconditionally, because the relationship has to be made safe before the issue can be solved, and you cannot solve a problem with someone who does not feel safe with you.

## Receive the repair when it comes

The other side of this is the harder part to talk about. When your spouse reaches for repair, receive it. A repair attempt is often clumsy. It comes as a half-apology, a joke, a hand on your back, a softer voice, an offer to make coffee. It does not arrive in the perfect words you wanted. Whether the repair gets received matters more than whether the fight was clean. If your spouse extends a hand and you slap it away because the apology was not complete enough, you have just taught them not to try.

So when you see the attempt, take it. You can come back to the unfinished business later. In the moment, take the hand.

## Do not skip past the hurt to the resolution

There is a temptation, especially for the conflict-avoidant, to rush to we are fine now before anyone has actually felt heard. Premature peace is its own wound. Before you move on, each of you should be able to say back what the other was actually feeling, not the position, the feeling underneath it. You felt unseen. You felt like I do not respect your work. When your spouse hears their own fear named accurately by you, the body finally comes the rest of the way down, and only then is the repair real.

## Let the cross stand behind it

We follow a God who made peace by absorbing the conflict instead of winning it, who took the wound rather than dealing it. Every time you choose to own your part instead of pressing your advantage, every time you take the wound instead of returning it, you are doing in miniature what was done for you. Paul says forgive one another as God in Christ forgave you. Not as they deserve. As you were forgiven, which is to say before they have fully earned it. That is the engine of every repair.

## This week

If you are in the silence right now, go first. Do not wait for them to come to you. Find the part that is yours, however small, and name it out loud and specifically, with no but attached. If you are not in a fight right now, agree on your re-entry sentence before you need it, the one that means I am flooded and I am coming back. Couples who fight without a way home keep getting lost. The ones who last are not the ones who never crossed the line. They are the ones who learned to come back fast, before the wound had time to harden into a wall.

title: How to Rekindle Desire in a Long Marriage
excerpt: Desire in a long marriage does not die because love faded. It cools because the conditions that fed it quietly disappeared, and the conditions can be rebuilt.
body:
Somewhere in a long marriage, often without either person deciding it, the fire goes low. Not out, usually. Low. You are partners, parents, co-managers of a complicated life, and the part of you that once could not keep your hands off this person has gone quiet, and you do not talk about it, because talking about it feels like an accusation, and not talking about it lets it keep cooling.

The church is often too embarrassed to help here, which is strange, because Scripture is not embarrassed at all. The Song of Songs is in the canon, an unblushing celebration of married desire, God's own answer to the lie that holiness is the enemy of passion. Paul tells married couples not to deprive one another, treating physical union as a mutual gift and a guarding of the marriage against the cold. The body is part of the covenant, not a distraction from it. So let us talk about it plainly.

## Desire is not a feeling that just shows up

The first lie we believe is that desire is spontaneous, that it should arrive on its own the way it did at the start, and if it does not, something is broken. At the start it was spontaneous because everything was new and you had endless unstructured time and your bodies had not yet been worn down by years of work and children and worry. That kind of desire was a gift of the season, and the season passed. It is not coming back on its own, and waiting for it is how a marriage waits itself into a permanent winter.

Mature desire is mostly responsive, not spontaneous. It does not show up first and then lead to closeness. It shows up because you created the closeness, and then the desire follows. This reverses everything. You do not wait to feel it before you tend it. You tend it, and the feeling comes back to meet you.

## Rebuild the conditions

Desire grows in specific soil, and in a long marriage that soil gets quietly paved over. Find what got paved and break it back up.

The first condition is attention. Desire needs to feel seen, and a spouse who has become invisible, who is only ever addressed about logistics, stops feeling like a person you want and starts feeling like a colleague. Look at your spouse again. Ask them a real question. Touch them in passing in a way that is not a request for anything. The Puritans, of all people, understood this, that romance is not a feeling that happens to you but a fire that has to be fed by attention and kindness, on purpose, and that love left untended cools.

The second condition is non-utilitarian touch. In a long marriage, touch becomes entirely functional, especially in the years of small children, all of it carrying and feeding and the brief logistics of the bed. When the only touch is functional, the body forgets the other language. Bring back the touch that asks for nothing, the long hug in the kitchen, the hand held on a walk. The body has to be reminded that it is desired and not just deployed.

The third condition is separateness, which sounds wrong and is true. Desire needs a little distance to cross. Two people who have fused completely, who do everything together and have no separate self left, can lose the gap that desire arches across. Have a life of your own, an interest, a friendship, a competence your spouse admires from a small distance. Watching your spouse be good at something, alive in something that is theirs, can reignite the wanting that total togetherness flattened.

## Talk about it without the accusation

The conversation feels dangerous because any version of I want more can land as you are failing me. So aim it at the marriage, not at your spouse. I miss us. I miss this part of us, and I want to find our way back to it, and I do not blame you for where it went, because I let it go too. Self-implication disarms the conversation. The moment your spouse hears that you are not prosecuting them, that you are inside the problem with them, the defensiveness drops and the real conversation can start.

And listen for what cooled it. Sometimes the desire went low because of resentment that never got cleared, or exhaustion that never got relieved, or a hurt around the body that never got spoken. Desire is honest. It often will not return until the thing blocking it gets named. The bedroom is frequently where the unaddressed rest of the marriage shows up.

## Guard the conditions like they matter

The practical part is unromantic and necessary. You will not stumble into the conditions. You have to protect them. A regular time when you are both awake enough to want each other and not running on the fumes of an exhausting day. A door that locks. A phone left in the other room. The couples who keep this alive across decades are not the ones who got lucky. They are the ones who treated it as something worth tending and refused to let it be the thing that always got cut when life got busy.

## This week

Do two small things. First, touch your spouse once a day this week in a way that asks for nothing, a real hug, a hand held, thirty seconds, no agenda. You are rebuilding the language. Second, sometime this week, say the gentle version of the true thing: I miss us, and I want to find our way back. Do not aim for a transformed marriage by Friday. Aim to break up a little of the paved ground, and to say the thing you have both been afraid to say. The fire did not go out. It went low for lack of tending, and tending is something you can begin again tonight.

title: How to Stay Married in the Baby Years
excerpt: No one warns you that the baby can come between you. The child does not threaten the marriage, but the way we organize our love around the child often does.
body:
No one warns you that the baby can come between you. They warn you about sleep and diapers and money. They do not warn you that one night, three months in, you will look across the room at the person you married and realize you have not had a real conversation in weeks, that you have become two exhausted people running a small institution together, and somewhere in the logistics the marriage went quiet and you did not notice it leave.

I have five sons. I am not writing this from theory. I am writing it from the years my wife and I nearly disappeared into the machinery of raising them, and from the slow work of finding each other on the other side.

## The marriage serves the children, not the other way around

The church sentimentalizes the family in a way that quietly sacrifices the marriage to the children, as if the marriage were merely the delivery system and not a thing with its own life. It is exactly backward. The most important thing you give your children is not your undivided attention. It is the sight of two parents who still love each other, because that is the only picture of covenant they will get up close, and they are watching it whether you mean for them to or not. Keep the marriage alive not at the expense of the children but as the deepest gift you give them.

## Do not let the mother and child fuse and the father drift

In the early months there is a real biological closeness between mother and infant, and it is good and it is not the problem. The problem is when it hardens into a permanent arrangement, when the mother becomes the gatekeeper and the father becomes the assistant who keeps getting it wrong until he stops trying. She ends up doing everything and resenting him for not helping. He ends up locked out and resenting the lock. Both are partly right.

The way out is counterintuitive. She has to let him do it badly, has to tolerate the diaper put on wrong and the outfit that does not match, because a father who is corrected at every turn will retreat. And he has to do it before he is asked. The father who waits to be told what to do has made his wife the manager of two children, one of whom is him, and no woman can carry that and stay tender.

## Refuse to let the marriage become a logistics meeting

Every conversation becomes a handoff. Who has pickup, did you call the pediatrician, we are out of formula. This is necessary and it is not connection, and the danger is mistaking the volume of words for intimacy. You can talk all day and never touch the other person's soul. Protect a kind of talk that is not about the kids. Ten minutes after they are down where you ask, not what is on the calendar, but how are you, actually, how is your heart in all this. If the only words between you are operational, you are running a business, and businesses do not love each other.

## Keep the touch that is not utilitarian

In this season two bodies get touched all day by people who need things from them, and by night the last thing either tired body wants is to be touched again. I am not only talking about sex, though that goes too. I mean the ordinary touch that says I still see you as my spouse and not just my co-worker, a hand held, a long hug in the kitchen that asks for nothing. When touch becomes entirely functional, the marriage loses the language of the body, and that language is hard to recover once it goes fully silent.

## See the invisible load

When children arrive, the labor in a home multiplies overnight, and how it gets divided becomes a quiet battleground. The danger is not unfairness so much as invisibility. One spouse carries a hundred small things that never get seen, the appointments tracked in their head, the shoes bought before the feet outgrew them, the birthday gift remembered on a Tuesday, and the other, genuinely unaware, thinks things run smoothly because they cannot see the labor that keeps them running.

The practice is not a perfectly equal split, which does not exist and which keeping score over will wreck you. The practice is seeing. The spouse carrying the invisible load needs to hear their partner say, I see what you are carrying, and I am not going to pretend it carries itself. That sentence does more than another load of laundry, because the loneliness was always the real wound.

## Do not wait out the season

The most dangerous plan is we will reconnect when they are older. The kids are not going to get less demanding for eighteen years. The toddler becomes the kid with three activities becomes the teenager whose life is a logistics nightmare of its own. The couples who reach the empty nest as strangers did not lose each other in one bad year. They lost each other one postponed conversation at a time across two decades, always meaning to reconnect later, until later arrived and there was no one across the table they recognized.

The work is not to wait out the season but to keep the marriage barely, stubbornly alive inside it, on whatever small budget the season allows. Not the grand romance you had before. A flame kept lit on almost nothing, which is its own discipline. Twenty minutes. A walk around the block while a neighbor watches the kids. A standing time, even fifteen minutes, fiercely guarded. The size matters less than the fact of it.

## This week

Do one thing for each other. For the one carrying the invisible load: your spouse names three specific things they know you carry that usually go unseen, out loud, this week. For both of you: find one fifteen-minute window where you talk about something that is not the children, even if you sit in the car in the driveway to do it. The children will not remember the spotless house. They will carry in their bodies the answer to one question they never asked out loud, whether love lasts, and they learn it from watching whether their father turns toward their mother or away.

title: How to Pray Together as a Couple
excerpt: Couples who long to pray together often do not, because the first attempt felt awkward and exposed. The awkwardness is the doorway, not the wall.
body:
Many Christian couples carry a quiet guilt about this. They believe they should pray together, they have heard the statistics about how rarely couples who pray together part ways, and they do not do it, or they did it for a week early in marriage and then it faded. They do not talk about why. The why is almost always the same. Praying together is one of the most exposed things two people can do, more exposed in some ways than the bedroom, and the first attempts felt so awkward that they quietly stopped.

I want to take the awkwardness seriously rather than shame you past it, because the shame is part of what keeps the practice dead.

## Why it feels so exposed

To pray out loud in front of your spouse is to let them hear what you actually believe, what you actually fear, what you actually want from God. It strips off the managed version of yourself. For a husband especially, who may carry an unspoken sense that he should be the spiritual leader and a private fear that he has no idea how, praying aloud risks exposing the gap. So he does not start, and she will not start because she does not want to embarrass him, and the silence becomes permanent and gets explained away as just not our thing.

Name this out loud to each other. The awkwardness shared is half disarmed. You can simply say, this feels strange to me and I do not really know how, and I want to do it anyway. That sentence, spoken between you, is already a kind of prayer.

## Start far smaller than you think

The great mistake is starting too big, deciding you will now pray together for twenty minutes every night, which lasts four days. Start with something so small it cannot fail. One sentence each, at one fixed moment. At the end of the day, before sleep, each of you prays one sentence out loud. Thank you for getting us through this hard day. Be with my brother who is sick. Help me be kinder tomorrow. That is enough. That is real prayer, and it is sustainable, and you can build on it once it has become a habit instead of an event.

Give it a fixed anchor so it does not depend on remembering. Hands held before the meal. The last thing before the light goes out. A short prayer in the car before you both leave for work. Attach it to a thing you already do every day and it will survive. Leave it floating and it will drift.

## A few simple forms

If one-sentence prayers feel too bare after a while, here are shapes that hold without requiring eloquence.

Pray the day back to God. Each of you names one thing you were grateful for that day and one thing you are worried about, and turns each into a short sentence to God. This doubles as a marriage check-in and a prayer at once, because to hear your spouse thank God for something and to hear what they are afraid of is to know them.

Pray Scripture. Open a psalm and read it slowly, a few verses each, and let the words be your prayer when your own run out. The Psalms have language for every state a marriage passes through, the grateful and the desperate and the angry, and praying them takes the pressure off having to compose something.

Pray for your children by name, one at a time. Few things bind two parents like kneeling, literally or otherwise, over the same child before God, naming the same hopes and the same fears for them. This is some of the most natural praying a couple will ever do, because the love is already there and only needs a direction.

## When you are not at peace

Here is the hard one. It is nearly impossible to pray honestly with someone you are at war with, which is exactly why Peter warns husbands that mistreating a wife will hinder their prayers. If you are cold toward each other, the shared prayer either dies or becomes a performance. Do not force a falsely warm prayer over a cold marriage. Instead, let the need to pray together drive you toward repair. Sometimes the most honest prayer a struggling couple can pray is short and true: God, we are not okay right now, and we do not know how to fix it, help us. That prayer, prayed while you are still hurting, is more real than any polished one, and God is not put off by it. He is drawn to it.

## Let it be ordinary

Resist the pressure to make this profound. Most faithful praying in a marriage is short, plain, repetitive, and unspectacular, two tired people saying a few true words to God before sleep, year after year. That is not a lesser version of the practice. That is the practice. The drama is not the point. The faithfulness is, the slow accumulation of a thousand small turnings toward God together, which over decades does something to a marriage that no single dramatic prayer could.

## This week

Tonight, before sleep, pray one sentence out loud, each of you. Just one. Tell your spouse first that it will feel strange and you want to do it anyway. Do not aim for a beautiful prayer. Aim for a true one and a short one. Then do it again tomorrow. The couples who pray together are almost never the eloquent ones. They are the ones who got past the first awkward week and let it become as ordinary as turning off the light.

title: How to Actually Forgive Your Spouse
excerpt: Forgiveness is not pretending it did not happen, and it is not a feeling that arrives on its own. It is a decision, often made before the feeling catches up.
body:
Two sinners cannot share a life without wounding each other, daily, in ways large and small, and a marriage is finally only as durable as its capacity to forgive. We know this in theory. In practice we are terrible at it, partly because no one ever taught us what forgiveness actually is, and so we confuse it with several things it is not and then resent it for failing to do what it was never meant to do.

Let me clear the ground first, because most of the trouble with forgiveness comes from misunderstanding it.

## What forgiveness is not

Forgiveness is not saying it did not matter. The opposite. You only forgive what was real, what cost you something. Minimizing the wound is not forgiveness, it is denial, and denial does not heal, it buries, and buried things do not stay buried.

Forgiveness is not the same as trust. You can forgive a spouse who lied to you and still require that trust be rebuilt over time through changed behavior. Forgiveness is given freely. Trust is earned back slowly. Confusing the two is how people get told to immediately trust someone who has given them no reason to, which is not grace, it is foolishness.

Forgiveness is not always reconciliation. Forgiveness takes one person. Reconciliation takes two, and requires the offender to own what they did. You can forgive someone who refuses to repent, but you cannot have full reconciliation with them, and you should not pretend you do.

And forgiveness is not a feeling. This is the one that traps people. They wait to feel forgiving, and the feeling does not come, and they conclude they have not forgiven and never will. Forgiveness is first a decision, a releasing of the debt, made by the will, often while the feelings are still raw. The feelings follow later, sometimes much later, sometimes in waves with relapses in between.

## What forgiveness is

Forgiveness is releasing the right to make them pay. That is the core of it. When someone wrongs you, they incur a debt, and you have a right to collect, by punishing, by withholding, by bringing it up, by keeping the wound on the books so you can charge interest on it for years. To forgive is to cancel the debt, to give up the right to collect, to absorb the cost yourself rather than extract it from them.

This is exactly what the cross is. Paul says, forgive one another as God in Christ forgave you. Not as they deserve. As you were forgiven, which is to say at someone else's cost, freely, before you had earned it. The reason a Christian can forgive a real wrong is not that the wrong was small but that their own enormous debt has already been cleared, and a person who has been forgiven much loses the standing to hold a small account against someone else. The unforgiving servant in Jesus' parable is not condemned for being wronged. He is condemned for choking a fellow servant over a few coins while standing forgiven of a fortune.

## How to actually do it

Name the wound specifically. Vague forgiveness does not work because vague wounds do not heal. Say to yourself, and if it is safe to the marriage, to your spouse, exactly what was done and exactly how it hurt. You said you would be there and you were not, and I felt alone and humiliated. You cannot release a debt you have not named.

Decide to release it. This is a definite act, often a spoken one, even if only to God. I release my right to make you pay for this. I will not bring it up as a weapon. I will not collect on it. This is the hinge. Everything before it is preparation and everything after it is follow-through, but this is where the forgiveness actually happens, in the will, before the feelings have moved.

Then keep deciding it. Forgiveness for a deep wound is not one decision but a hundred, because the wound will resurface, the memory will rise with the old fire on it, and the resentment will ask for the right back. Each time, you release it again. This is not failure. This is what forgiving a serious wrong looks like from the inside, a daily handing back of a debt you keep instinctively picking up. Over time the grip loosens. The feelings catch up. The wound becomes a scar instead of an open thing.

## When the wound is severe

For betrayal, for the deep wounds, forgiveness does not mean you skip the process of grieving and rebuilding. It does not mean you cannot require honesty, accountability, sometimes outside help. Forgiveness and consequences can coexist. You can forgive and still say, I forgive you, and we are going to counseling, and you are going to rebuild my trust, because the forgiveness is about my heart and the rebuilding is about our marriage, and both have to happen.

And a word of caution: forgiveness is not a tool for keeping someone trapped in danger. If you are being abused, forgiving in your heart is one thing, and it does not require you to stay in harm's way or to pretend the danger is not real. Get safe first. Forgiveness was never meant to be a chain.

## This week

Take the one resentment you keep picking back up, the wound you have rehearsed a hundred times. Name it specifically, on paper or out loud to God, exactly what was done and how it hurt. Then make the actual decision: I release my right to make them pay for this. You will have to make it again tomorrow, and the day after. Make it anyway. The couples who last are not the ones who stopped wounding each other. They are the ones who never stopped forgiving, who kept the account short because they remembered how long their own account with God had been, and how completely it was cleared.

title: How to Protect a Weekly Date Night
excerpt: Date night fails not because couples do not value it, but because everything else is louder. Protecting it is a discipline, not a romance.
body:
Almost every couple agrees a regular date night is a good idea. Almost no couple manages to keep one. The reason is not that they do not love each other. The reason is that a date night is the single most cancelable thing on the calendar. The work meeting is fixed. The kids' game is fixed. The dentist is fixed. The one block of time set aside for the marriage itself is the one block that flexes every time life pushes, and life pushes constantly, so the marriage gets the leftover scraps of exhausted attention, week after week, until there is nothing left to give it.

Protecting a date night is therefore not mainly about romance. It is about discipline, about treating the marriage as a fixed appointment rather than the slack in the schedule. Here is how couples who keep one actually do it.

## Make it recurring and fixed

A date that has to be negotiated every week will not survive, because the negotiation is friction, and friction is what kills habits. Pick a day and make it standing. Every Thursday. The first and third Friday. Whatever fits, but it does not move, and it does not require a fresh decision each week. The decision was made once. Now it just is what Thursday is.

Defend it like a bill that is due. When something tries to claim the time, the default answer is no, that is our night, the way you would say no, that money is already spent. Most things that look urgent are not, and the ones that genuinely are will be rare enough that protecting the night the other fifty weeks still works.

## Solve childcare permanently, not weekly

For couples with young children, childcare is where date night dies, because arranging a sitter every single week is exhausting enough that you stop bothering. Solve it once. A standing sitter for the same evening every week. A swap with another couple, you take their kids one week and they take yours the next, which costs nothing and gives both marriages a night. Grandparents on a regular schedule if you have them nearby. The point is to remove the weekly decision, because every decision is a chance to skip it.

If money is tight, the date does not have to cost anything. Put the kids to bed and have coffee on the porch. Walk after dark. The expense was never the point. The protected, undistracted attention is the point, and that is free.

## Protect the quality, not just the slot

Getting the time on the calendar is half the battle. The other half is what you do with it, because a date night spent on phones, or spent entirely on logistics, is just the marriage's business meeting in a nicer room.

Leave the phones in the car or in a drawer. The phone is the great thief of presence, and a couple who spends date night each scrolling has technically had a date and actually had nothing. Agree on it in advance so neither of you has to police the other in the moment.

And ban the logistics. The kids' schedule, the house repairs, the budget, all of it is off limits on date night, because if you allow it in, it will eat the whole evening, since logistics is always the loudest thing. The date is for the two of you as people, not as co-managers. Talk about something other than the institution you are running together. Ask each other the kinds of questions you asked when you were getting to know each other, because you have both changed since then and there is more to know.

## Lower the bar so it survives

The enemy of the regular date is the belief that it has to be special. A grand date is expensive and hard to arrange, so it happens rarely, and rarely is not what a marriage needs. A marriage needs frequently. An ordinary, repeatable, low-effort date that happens every week does more than an elaborate one that happens twice a year, the way a small meal every day sustains a body better than a feast once a season.

So make it boringly sustainable. Same restaurant is fine. Same walk is fine. The familiarity is not the problem. The consistency is the whole gift. You are not trying to manufacture a highlight reel. You are trying to keep a standing weekly appointment with the most important person in your life, and the keeping is what matters, not the spectacle.

## Why this is not optional

It is easy to file date night under nice if you can manage it. But the marriages that drift apart almost never decide to. They drift one postponed evening at a time, always meaning to reconnect when things calm down, and things do not calm down. The weekly date is the structural defense against that drift, a fixed point where the two of you are forced back into each other's company as people and not as the staff of a shared enterprise. It is not a luxury on top of a healthy marriage. It is one of the things that keeps a marriage healthy.

## This week

Pick the day now, before you finish reading. Put it on both calendars as recurring, not as a one-time event. Then solve the childcare for it permanently this week, a standing sitter, a swap with friends, or grandparents, so you never have to arrange it again. Make the first one cheap and simple so the bar is low enough to actually clear. You are not planning a romance. You are setting a fixed appointment with your marriage, and then keeping it, every week, long after the week you do not feel like it, which is precisely the week it matters most.

title: How to Love a Spouse Who Has Gone Cold
excerpt: When a marriage goes cold from one side, the temptation is to match the coldness. The harder and better road is to keep loving without a guarantee.
body:
There is a particular loneliness in lying next to someone who has gone cold. Not cruel, usually. Just absent. The warmth has drained out of them, the affection, the interest, and you do not know exactly when it happened or why, and your attempts to reach them keep landing on a surface that does not give. You are still married. You are not still close. And the worst part is that you cannot fix it alone, because it takes two to be close and only one to be distant.

I want to be honest with you about how hard this is before I say anything else, because cheap encouragement is an insult to people in this situation. This is one of the heaviest things a person can carry, and there is no technique that guarantees a thaw. What I can offer is a way to love and to stay whole while you do not yet know how it ends.

## First, try to find out why

Coldness is a symptom, not a cause, and the cause matters. A spouse goes cold for reasons, even if neither of you can name them yet. Accumulated resentment that never got cleared. A hurt you do not know you caused. Depression, which can drain warmth out of a person and has nothing to do with you, though it feels like it does. Exhaustion past the point of having anything to give. Sometimes something more serious, an affair of the heart or the body, a foot already partway out the door. The right response is different for each, so before you decide how to love them, try to understand what you are loving them through.

Ask, gently and without accusation. Not what is wrong with you, which is an attack, but I have felt a distance between us and I do not want to assume I know why, and I want to understand. Then be quiet long enough for an answer. You may not get one the first time. Ask again, another day, without making the asking itself a pressure.

## Do not match the coldness

The strongest pull, when someone goes cold, is to go cold back. To protect yourself by withdrawing first, to stop reaching so you stop getting hurt, to give them the distance they seem to want. It feels like dignity. It is mostly self-protection, and it accelerates exactly the thing you fear, because now both of you are withdrawing and the marriage cools twice as fast.

This is where the gospel asks something hard and specific. We love a God who kept loving while we were still cold to him, who did not wait for us to warm up before he moved toward us. Romans says that while we were still enemies, Christ died for us. The pattern of that love is movement toward distance, not away from it. To keep loving a cold spouse, in small and undramatic ways, without the guarantee of return, is one of the truest imitations of Christ a person can offer, and one of the most costly.

This does not mean groveling or chasing. It means refusing to let their coldness set your temperature. You keep the small warmth alive, the kind word, the made coffee, the touch on the shoulder, not as a transaction to earn warmth back, but because that is who you have decided to be regardless of what comes back. There is a strange freedom in this. When you love without requiring a return, the other person's coldness loses some of its power to control you.

## Stay whole while you wait

You cannot pour love from an empty self, and a person being slowly frozen out will run dry if they have no other source. So do not make your cold spouse the only well you drink from. This is where the rest of your life matters enormously, the friendships, the church, the work that has meaning, the God who promised never to leave or forsake even when a spouse has. A believer is anchored not in a spouse's responsiveness but in a Father who will never go cold, and that anchor is what keeps you from being destroyed by a marriage that is not, right now, giving you anything.

Do not isolate. The instinct in a cold marriage is to hide it, out of shame and loyalty, and the hiding leaves you alone with it. Find one or two safe people, a wise friend, a pastor, who can hold this with you and remind you who you are when the daily coldness starts to make you doubt it.

## Know the limits, and know the line

Keeping faith with a cold spouse is not the same as accepting harm. There is a difference, and it is the most important distinction in this whole piece. Coldness is one thing. Cruelty is another. If your spouse is not merely distant but controlling, frightening, or abusive, if there is violence, intimidation, or a fear in you about your safety, then this is no longer the situation I have been describing, and the counsel changes entirely. You do not owe an abuser the patient, hopeful love this article describes. You owe yourself and your children safety first. Get to a safe place and get help. In the United States you can reach the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 800-799-7233, any hour. Forgiveness and faithfulness were never meant to be a chain that binds a person to harm.

For a marriage that is cold rather than dangerous, there is still a limit to what one person can carry alone, and reaching that limit is not a failure. If your reaching gets no response over a long season, it is right and wise to ask your spouse to go to counseling with you, and right to go yourself even if they will not. Loving a cold spouse does not mean accepting that nothing can change. It means refusing to give up on change while also refusing to let the waiting destroy you.

## This week

Do two things. First, find one moment to ask the gentle question, I have felt a distance, and I want to understand, not to accuse, and then listen without defending. Second, name one source of life outside the marriage that you have let go dry, a friendship, your time with God, something that is yours, and take one step back toward it this week, because you cannot keep loving from empty. And if what you are facing is not coldness but danger, do not wait. Get safe first. That is not the failure of love. It is the floor beneath it.

title: How to Handle In-Laws (Leaving and Cleaving)
excerpt: Much marital misery is really an unfinished leaving. A man shall leave his father and mother, and we skip that verb in our hurry to the next one.
body:
The verse everyone knows says a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh. Three verbs, and we rush past the first two to get to the third. Leave. Hold fast. One flesh. The in-law trouble that strains so many marriages is almost always a failure at the first verb. Someone did not leave. They got married and stayed, in the ways that count, loyal to a parent in a way that left their spouse on the outside, and no amount of love at the third verb can fix a failure at the first.

This is not about loving your parents less. Honor your father and mother is a commandment that does not expire at the wedding. It is about reordering, about a new primary loyalty being formed, a new household that the old loyalties now arrange themselves around rather than rule.

## What leaving actually means

Leaving is not geographic and it is not the end of the relationship with your parents. It is a shift in allegiance. Before marriage your primary human loyalty was to the family you came from. After marriage it is to the spouse. This means that when there is a conflict between your parent's wishes and your marriage's good, the marriage wins, and your parent does not get a vote that outranks your spouse's.

You can tell whether someone has left by what happens under pressure. When the mother criticizes the wife, does the husband defend his wife or fall silent and let it stand. When the father disapproves of a decision the couple made together, does the son hold the line with his spouse or quietly side with his father and leave his wife exposed. The spouse who has not left keeps siding, in the small moments, with the family of origin, and the married spouse feels it as a betrayal even when nothing dramatic is said, because they have learned they are not actually first.

## The unleft spouse, and the one married to them

If you are the one who has not fully left, the tell is usually a particular fear, the fear of your parent's disappointment. You make decisions, or fail to make them, to avoid a mother's hurt look or a father's cooled approval, and your spouse pays for it. The work here is to grow up the rest of the way, to be able to disappoint your parent for the sake of your marriage without it feeling like the end of the world. That is what leaving costs, and it is a cost you have to be willing to pay, repeatedly, in small moments, until your spouse knows without question that they come first.

If you are married to someone who has not left, the temptation is to fight the in-laws directly, and it almost always backfires, because attacking your spouse's parent forces them to choose, and a person who has not finished leaving will instinctively defend the parent. The wiser move is to aim at your spouse, gently, not at the parent. Not your mother is impossible, which makes him defensive, but I need to know that you and I decide things together, and that when it matters, you are on my side. Make it about the loyalty, not about the parent's character. The goal is to help your spouse leave, not to win a war against their family.

## Set the boundary together, present it as one

The single most important practical rule with in-laws is that the boundary is set by the couple together and presented as a united front, and ideally communicated by the spouse whose parent it is. The husband talks to his parents. The wife talks to hers. This protects everyone. It keeps the in-law from feeling attacked by the outsider who married in, and it forces the couple to decide together rather than one spouse managing the other's family alone.

When the boundary gets crossed, the parent should hear it from their own child, not from the in-law. Mom, we have decided we are doing our own Christmas morning this year, and we will come over in the afternoon. From the son, that is a family reordering. From the daughter-in-law, it is an insult and a power struggle. Same boundary, completely different result, depending on who carries it.

## A few common fault lines

The holidays are the classic battleground, two families each assuming they get the couple, and the couple torn in half trying to satisfy both. The answer is that the new household decides its own holidays and then informs the families, kindly and clearly and early, rather than asking permission and getting trapped between two sets of expectations.

Money from parents is another quiet trap, because money often comes with strings, spoken or not, and a couple dependent on a parent's generosity can find that the parent has bought a vote in the marriage. Receive help with open eyes. If the gift comes with control attached, the gift may cost more than it gives.

And the criticism of a spouse by a parent is the one that wounds longest. A parent who runs down your spouse to you is asking you to betray your marriage, even if they would never call it that. The leaving spouse does not laugh along or stay silent. They say, gently and once, that is my husband, my wife, you are talking about, and I need you to speak about them with respect. You defend the absent spouse to your own family. That is what holding fast looks like when they are not in the room.

## Honor without obeying

None of this is permission to dishonor your parents. You can honor a parent and still not obey them, still not let them rule a marriage they are not part of. Honor means respect, care, presence, gratitude, the cup of cold water in their old age. It does not mean the surrendering of your marriage's authority to them. Jesus himself, at the wedding in Cana, gently set a boundary with his own mother while still honoring her. The two are not enemies. A grown child can hold a parent in deep love and still make unmistakably clear where their first loyalty now lies.

## This week

Have one conversation with your spouse, alone, with no in-law in the room. Ask each other a single honest question: is there any place where you feel I have not fully left, where you feel my family comes before you. Then listen without defending, because the defending is the very reflex that proves the point. Pick one boundary you have both wanted and have been afraid to set, and agree that the spouse whose parent it is will carry it, kindly and clearly, this week. Leaving is not a one-time act at the altar. It is a thousand small moments of choosing your spouse out loud, and your marriage will know, by the end of this week, whether you are willing to do it.

title: How to Know When to Get Help
excerpt: Most couples wait far too long to get help, treating counseling as the last stop before the lawyer. The wisest couples go early, while there is still warmth to build on.
body:
The average couple in trouble waits years before they get help, and by the time they finally walk into a counselor's office, the damage has compounded for so long that the work is twice as hard as it needed to be. We treat marriage counseling as the emergency room, the place you go when the marriage is already coding, when in fact it is far more like a regular check-up, something the healthiest couples do early and without shame, while there is still plenty to build on. The stigma costs marriages. Let me try to dismantle it.

First, the most important thing: there is one category that is not about counseling at all, and I am going to put it before everything else because it cannot wait behind the other considerations.

## If there is abuse, this is different

Abuse is not a marriage problem to be worked on together in a counselor's office. It is a safety problem, and the rules are different. If your spouse is violent, if you are afraid of them, if there is intimidation, control of your money or movements, threats, or any physical harm, do not start with couples counseling, which can actually be dangerous in an abusive dynamic because it can be used against the victim afterward. Start with getting safe. Tell someone you trust. Make a plan. In the United States, the National Domestic Violence Hotline is available any hour at 800-799-7233, and they can help you think through safety even if you are not sure it counts. It counts. The covenant of marriage was never meant to be a chain that binds a person to harm, and a God who hates violence does not require you to stay in reach of it. Get safe first. Everything else in this article assumes a marriage that is struggling, not one that is dangerous.

## The signs it is time, for an ordinary struggling marriage

Go early, not at the end. Here are the signals that it is time, and notice that none of them require things to be catastrophic.

The same fight keeps running, under different names, and you cannot get to the bottom of it on your own. When a couple has been circling the identical conflict for months or years, going nowhere, that is exactly the kind of stuck a skilled outside person is trained to break. You are not failing by needing help to see what you cannot see from inside it.

You have stopped being able to talk about the hard things at all, and the silence between you has become the safer option. A marriage where the real subjects have become off-limits is a marriage slowly going underground, and that quiet is more dangerous than the loud fights.

Contempt has crept in, the eye roll, the running someone down, the settled conviction that your spouse is the problem with your life. Contempt is the most corrosive thing a marriage can carry, and once it has set in, couples rarely reverse it alone.

There has been a betrayal, of the body or of trust or of the finances, and you are trying to rebuild and cannot find the way. Rebuilding after betrayal is some of the hardest work a marriage does, and almost no one should attempt it without help.

Or simply that you have drifted into parallel lives, two people running a household with no closeness left, and you both feel it and neither of you knows how to find your way back. You do not have to be in crisis to deserve help. The drift itself is reason enough.

## Disarming the objections

Let me take the resistance seriously, because I have felt it. The first objection is that getting help means admitting failure. It is the opposite. Getting help is what people do who refuse to let the marriage fail, who take it seriously enough to bring in the best resources they can find. We do not call it failure when someone sees a doctor for a body they cannot heal alone. The marriage is the load-bearing wall of an entire life. It is strange that we will pay for a mechanic and balk at help for the thing the whole house rests on.

The second objection is that a good Christian marriage should not need outside help, that we should be able to pray our way through. God works through means, through doctors and teachers and wise counselors, and pretending otherwise is not faith, it is pride. Proverbs says there is wisdom in many counselors. Seeking help is not a failure of trust in God. It is often the form your trust takes.

The third is that we cannot afford it. There are sliding-scale counselors, there are pastors trained for this, there are church-based ministries, there are good books and structured resources for couples who genuinely cannot reach a professional. Cost is a real barrier and there are more doors through it than most people check. And weighed against what the slow failure of a marriage costs, financially and otherwise, the help is almost always the cheaper road.

## What good help looks like

Not all help is equal, so choose with care. Look for someone who takes your faith seriously if your faith is central to your marriage, and who also has real training, not only good intentions. Look for someone who will hold both of you accountable rather than taking sides. And give it a real chance, more than one session, because the first session is mostly the counselor learning the shape of things. If after a fair try a particular counselor is not helping, it is fine to find another. The wrong counselor is not proof that counseling cannot help you.

## This week

If there is any abuse or fear in your marriage, the only step this week is toward safety, not toward couples work. Tell one safe person, and call the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 800-799-7233 if you need help thinking it through. For an ordinary struggling marriage, the step is smaller and you can take it this week: name to your spouse that you would like to get help, framed not as you need fixing but as I do not want us to keep circling this alone, and I think someone could help us see it. Then make one inquiry, a call to a counselor, a note to your pastor, a search for a sliding-scale clinic. Do not wait until you are at the lawyer's door. The couples who get the most from help are almost always the ones who went before they thought they had to.
